paragraphs.text: In 1985, the J. Paul Getty Museum acquired what it believed to be a Greek kouros (a statue of a naked youth) dating from the Archaic period (650-480 B.C.E.), estimating the date of origin as approximately 530 B.C.E. The Getty Kouros's authenticity soon came into question, however. Supporters cited scientific analyses suggesting that the statue's marble is consistent with marble known to have come from ancient Greek quarries and that its surface shows chemical changes consistent with long. term burial. Some scholars also argue that peculiar inconsistencies in the statue's style—it incorporates features from different regions and periods—could reflect a transitional moment in Greek sculpture.

paragraphs.text: Skeptics contend that these inconsistencies undermine the case for authenticity. The Kouros combines traits from several other known sixth-century B.C.E. kouroi in a way that appears too eclectic to be genuine. To these observers, the statue looks like a modern forger's creation—a confused imitation of Greek Archaic elements rather than the genuine product of a coherent sculptural tradition. Furthermore, scientists recognize that modern forgers can artificially age marble.
